title: A decrease, a signed change, and a conversion
question: What has the argument identified, and which way does the change point?
recap: The positive mass lost is L/c²; the signed body-mass change is −L/c².
premises: The low-speed coefficient identification from the preceding step.
limitations: This calculation determines a change, not an absolute internal energy.
Einstein’s printed constants and modern values are kept in separate calculations.

overview.text: The emitting body loses inertia. A positive amount lost and a negative signed change describe the same event. The wider claim about energy content goes beyond this particular symmetric-emission calculation.

full.spoken: The mass before minus the mass after is positive L over c squared; the signed final-minus-initial change is negative L over c squared.

full.text: The conclusion here is a difference. It does not retroactively fill the unknown energy boxes with mc². The paper goes on to infer a broader relation between energy content and inertia; that generalization should remain distinguishable from the calculation that led to it.

Its numerical conversion uses a rounded light-speed-squared factor of 9 × 10²⁰ in centimetre-second units, so energy in erg gives mass in grams. The kinetic-energy laboratory keeps that historical constant set separate from the modern SI value. A unit conversion changes the description of the result, not the physical event.

items: From the small-speed comparison, m₀ − m₁ = L/c². L is the light energy emitted, measured in the rest frame, and it is positive, so the difference is positive: the body’s mass after the emission is the smaller one.
The signed change is the final mass minus the initial mass, Δm = m₁ − m₀. It is the negative of the difference above:

steps.spoken: The mass before minus the mass after is positive L over c squared; the signed final-minus-initial change is negative L over c squared.

items: In the historical units energy is in erg, mass in grams, and c² is the rounded printed factor 9 × 10²⁰, in centimetres squared per second squared. An emission of L = 9 × 10²⁰ erg would lower the mass by 9 × 10²⁰ erg divided by 9 × 10²⁰ cm²/s², which is 1 gram.

In modern SI units energy is in joules and mass in kilograms, and c = 299 792 458 metres per second exactly, so c² is about 8.99 × 10¹⁶ m²/s². An emission of 1 joule lowers the mass by 1/c², about 1.11 × 10⁻¹⁷ kilogram.
Never divide an energy in erg by an SI value of c², or joules by the printed factor: convert the units first. A unit conversion changes how the result is described, not the physical event.

The result is a difference between two masses. It does not fill the unknown energies E₀ and E₁ with mc², and the paper’s broader relation between energy content and inertia is a further inference, kept separate from this calculation.
A finite-speed estimate such as 2L(γ − 1)/v² at some nonzero speed is not this mass decrease; only its zero-speed limit is.

margin.text: In modern theory invariant mass depends on the chosen system boundary; total energy also depends on the frame. The modern rest-energy relation is not used as a premise of this explanatory route.
